preamble.summary: Seven brothers and their mother are arrested and tortured for refusing to eat pork. One by one, each brother speaks a defiant confession before being executed with increasing cruelty — tongues cut out, hands and feet amputated, scalps torn off, bodies fried in pans. Each speech affirms resurrection hope: God who gave life will restore it. The mother's speech (vv. 22-23, 27-29) contains the first explicit biblical statement of creation ex nihilo (7:28) and the most powerful maternal theology in scripture. The chapter closes with the mother's own death.
preamble.remarkable: This is arguably the most theologically influential chapter in the deuterocanonical literature. It contains: (1) the earliest explicit biblical reference to bodily resurrection (vv. 9, 11, 14, 23, 29); (2) the first clear statement of creation from nothing (v. 28: 'ex nihilo fecit illa Deus'); (3) a mother's theology of gestation and creation that links human motherhood to divine creativity (vv. 22-23); (4) the principle that the torturer's power is limited to the body while God's extends to eternity. The seven brothers became the 'Holy Maccabees' venerated in both Catholic and Orthodox traditions, and their mother ('the Maccabean Mother') became a model for the Virgin Mary in early Christian art.
preamble.friction: The Latin 'ex nihilo' in verse 28 is one of the most consequential phrases in the history of theology. We render it directly as 'from nothing,' preserving the philosophical weight that subsequent Christian theology built upon it. The description of the tortures is graphic in the Latin; we render it fully because the specificity of the suffering is part of the theological witness — the body that is destroyed is the same body that will be raised.
preamble.connections: The resurrection theology connects forward to Daniel 12:2-3, Romans 8:11, 1 Corinthians 15, and Hebrews 11:35 ('others were tortured, not accepting deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection' — a direct reference to this chapter). Creation ex nihilo (v. 28) becomes the foundation for the Christian doctrine developed in the Nicene Creed. The mother's speech echoes Hannah (1 Samuel 2) and anticipates Mary's Magnificat (Luke 1:46-55). The seven brothers are commemorated liturgically on August 1 in the Catholic calendar.

verses.text_latin: Contigit autem et septem fratres una cum matre sua adprehensos compelli a rege edere contra fas carnes porcinas flagris et taureis cruciatos.
verses.rendering: It happened also that seven brothers were arrested together with their mother and were compelled by the king to eat pork in violation of the law, being tortured with whips and leather straps.
translator_notes: The scene is set with economical brutality: seven brothers, their mother, the king himself present, the demand for pork, the torture already underway. 'Contra fas' (against divine law) frames the refusal as a matter of cosmic right, not personal preference.

key_terms.note: Fas is divine/natural law as opposed to ius (human/civil law). The brothers are being asked to violate the cosmic moral order.
Taurea — whips or straps made of bull hide, instruments of severe corporal punishment.

verses.text_latin: Unus autem ex illis qui erat primus sic ait: Quid quaeris et quid vis discere a nobis? Parati sumus mori magis quam patrias Dei leges praevaricari.
verses.rendering: One of them, the eldest, spoke thus: 'What do you seek? What do you wish to learn from us? We are prepared to die rather than transgress the ancestral laws of God.'
translator_notes: The first brother's speech is brief and absolute: death before transgression. 'Parati sumus mori' (we are prepared to die) — the plural includes all seven brothers in a collective declaration.

key_terms.note: The Torah as both ancestral heritage (patrias) and divine legislation (Dei leges) — the double ground of obedience.

verses.text_latin: Iratus itaque rex iussit sartagines et ollas aeneas succendi quibus statim succensis.
verses.rendering: The king, enraged, ordered pans and bronze cauldrons to be heated. When they were immediately heated,
translator_notes: The instruments of torture: frying pans and bronze cauldrons. The escalation from whips to burning implements marks the king's increasing fury.

key_terms.note: Frying pans used as instruments of torture — the domestic cooking implement turned to demonic purpose.

verses.text_latin: Iussit ei qui prior fuerat loqui amputari linguam et cute capitis abstracta summas quoque manus et pedes ei praecidi ceteris eius fratribus et matre inspicientibus.
verses.rendering: He commanded that the tongue of the one who had spoken first be cut out, and that the skin of his head be torn off, and that the extremities of his hands and feet be cut off, while his remaining brothers and his mother looked on.
translator_notes: The first brother is systematically mutilated: tongue (for his defiant speech), scalp, hands, and feet — all in front of his family. The forced witnessing is part of the torture, designed to break the others' resolve.

verses.text_latin: Et cum iam per omnia inutilis factus esset iussit ignem admoveri et adhuc spirantem torreri in sartagine. In qua cum diu cruciaretur ceteri una cum matre invicem se hortabantur mori fortiter.
verses.rendering: And when he had been rendered completely helpless, the king ordered the fire to be brought near and commanded that he be roasted alive in the pan while he still breathed. As he was tortured at length, the others, together with their mother, encouraged one another to die bravely.
translator_notes: The first brother is burned alive. Meanwhile, the rest encourage each other — the mother is specifically noted as part of this mutual encouragement. The family unit holds together under the worst extremity.

key_terms.note: Fortiter mori — the brave death, the Jewish-Hellenistic ideal of courageous faithfulness unto death.

verses.text_latin: Dicentes: Dominus Deus aspiciet veritatem et consolabitur in nobis quemadmodum in protestatione cantici declaravit Moyses: Et in servis suis consolabitur.
verses.rendering: They said, 'The Lord God sees the truth and will have compassion on us, as Moses declared in the song of protest: And he will have compassion on his servants.'
translator_notes: The brothers cite Deuteronomy 32:36 — the Song of Moses — as their biblical warrant. God 'sees the truth' (aspiciet veritatem) when human judges refuse to, and he will vindicate his servants.

key_terms.note: God as the true witness and judge who sees what human courts refuse to acknowledge.
Consolari — to comfort, console, have compassion. God's response to his servants' suffering is compassion, not indifference.

verses.text_latin: Mortuo itaque primo hoc modo alterum ducebant ad illudendum et cute capitis cum capillis abstracta interrogabant si manducaret priusquam toto corpore per membra singula puniretur.
verses.rendering: After the first had died in this way, they brought the second forward to be mocked. And tearing off the skin of his head with his hair, they asked whether he would eat before being punished limb by limb throughout his whole body.
translator_notes: The second brother faces the same pattern: scalping, the demand to eat, the threat of dismemberment. Each brother's ordeal is both individual and cumulative.

verses.text_latin: At ille respondens patria voce dixit: Non faciam. Propter quod et iste sequenti loco primi tormenta suscepit.
verses.rendering: But he answered in the ancestral language, 'I will not.' For this reason he too, in his turn, underwent the torments of the first.
translator_notes: 'Patria voce' (in the ancestral language) — Hebrew or Aramaic, not Greek. The choice of language is itself an act of resistance: even in death, they refuse to speak the tongue of the oppressor.

key_terms.note: Speaking Hebrew or Aramaic rather than Greek — linguistic resistance to Hellenization.

verses.text_latin: Et cum in ultimo spiritu iam esset ait: Tu quidem scelestissime in praesenti vita nos perdis sed Rex mundi defunctos nos pro suis legibus in aeternae vitae resurrectione suscitabit.
verses.rendering: And when he was at his last breath, he said, 'You, most wicked of men, destroy us in this present life, but the King of the world will raise us up to an everlasting renewal of life, since we have died for his laws.'
translator_notes: THE pivotal verse: the second brother declares bodily resurrection. 'Rex mundi' (King of the world) — God as cosmic sovereign, contrasted with the earthly king who only has power to destroy. 'In aeternae vitae resurrectione' (in the resurrection of eternal life) is the clearest resurrection statement in the Hebrew Bible/deuterocanonical literature before Daniel 12:2.

key_terms.note: God as the true king, whose sovereignty extends over life and death — in deliberate contrast to the Seleucid 'king' who can only kill.
The resurrection to eternal life — the earliest explicit biblical statement of this hope, foundational for both Jewish and Christian eschatology.

verses.text_latin: Post hunc tertius illuditur et linguam postulatus cito protulit et manus constanter extendit.
verses.rendering: After him the third was mocked. When asked, he quickly put out his tongue and bravely stretched out his hands,
translator_notes: The third brother actively presents his tongue and hands for mutilation — not passively enduring but actively offering his body. This voluntary self-offering transforms the execution into a kind of sacrifice.

verses.text_latin: Et cum fiducia ait: E caelo ista possideo sed propter Dei leges nunc haec ipsa despicio quoniam ab ipso me ea recepturum spero.
verses.rendering: And he said with confidence, 'I received these from heaven, but for the sake of the laws of God I now despise them, because from him I hope to receive them back again.'
translator_notes: The third brother's theology of the body: (1) the body comes from God ('e caelo ista possideo'); (2) it can be surrendered for God's laws ('propter Dei leges despicio'); (3) it will be restored by God ('ab ipso recepturum spero'). This is resurrection as restoration — the same body given back.

key_terms.note: The body as divine gift — hands and tongue are possessions received from God, which God can restore.

key_terms.rendered_as: I hope to receive them back
key_terms.note: Resurrection hope expressed as confident expectation of bodily restoration.

verses.text_latin: Ita ut rex ipse et qui cum eo erant mirarentur adulescentis animum quod tamquam nihilum duceret cruciatus.
verses.rendering: So that the king himself and those with him marveled at the young man's spirit, because he regarded the sufferings as nothing.
translator_notes: Even the torturer is impressed — a detail that underscores the supernatural quality of the brothers' courage. Their contempt for suffering is itself a testimony.

verses.text_latin: Et hoc ita defuncto quartum vexabant similiter torquentes.
verses.rendering: When this one too had died, they tormented the fourth in the same way, subjecting him to similar torture.
translator_notes: The repetition — 'similarly, in the same way' — creates a liturgical rhythm. Each death follows the same pattern, building cumulative weight.

verses.text_latin: Et cum iam esset ad mortem dixit ita: Potius est ab hominibus morti datos spem expectare a Deo iterum ab ipso resuscitandos tibi enim resurrectio ad vitam non erit.
verses.rendering: And when he was near death, he spoke thus: 'It is better, when given over to death by men, to await the hope from God of being raised again by him. For you, there will be no resurrection to life.'
translator_notes: The fourth brother adds a negative corollary: the persecutor will NOT be raised to life. Resurrection is not universal but conditional on faithfulness. This creates a two-track eschatology: resurrection for the righteous, permanent death for the wicked.

key_terms.note: Resurrection specifically 'to life' — implying that there is another kind of resurrection (to judgment) or no resurrection at all for the wicked.
The passive voice: God is the agent of resurrection; the dead are raised by divine action.

verses.text_latin: Et cum admovissent quintum vexabant eum. At ille respiciens in eum dixit:
verses.rendering: When they brought forward the fifth and began to torment him, he looked at the king and said,
translator_notes: The fifth brother directly addresses the king — eyeball to eyeball defiance.

verses.text_latin: Potestatem inter homines habens cum sis corruptibilis facis quod vis noli autem putare genus nostrum a Deo esse derelictum.
verses.rendering: 'You have authority among mortals, though you yourself are mortal. You do what you wish. But do not think that our people have been forsaken by God.'
translator_notes: The fifth brother relativizes the king's power: he has authority but only within the mortal realm, and he is himself mortal. The assurance that God has not forsaken the nation echoes 6:16.

key_terms.note: The king is corruptibilis — subject to decay and death, just like those he tortures.

verses.text_latin: Tu autem patiens esto et videbis magnam potestatem ipsius qua te et semen tuum torquebit.
verses.rendering: 'Be patient, and you will see his great power, by which he will torment you and your descendants.'
translator_notes: A prophetic threat: the tormentor will himself be tormented, and his dynasty with him. This was fulfilled when Antiochus IV died horribly (chapter 9) and his son was murdered.

verses.text_latin: Post hunc ducebant sextum et is mori incipiens ait: Noli frustra errare nos enim propter nosmetipsos haec patimur peccantes in Deum nostrum et digna miratione facta sunt.
verses.rendering: After him they brought the sixth, and as he was about to die, he said, 'Do not be deceived in vain. For we suffer these things because of ourselves, having sinned against our God; and astounding things have been done.'
translator_notes: The sixth brother introduces a penitential dimension: the suffering is partly deserved because of the nation's sins. This is not fatalism but covenantal theology — sin has consequences, but those consequences do not negate God's ultimate purpose.

key_terms.note: The acknowledgment that Israel's suffering has a penitential dimension — not pure innocence but covenantal discipline.

verses.text_latin: Tu autem ne existimes tibi impune futurum quod adversus Deum pugnare temptaveris.
verses.rendering: 'But do not think that you will go unpunished for having attempted to fight against God.'
translator_notes: The sixth brother warns the king that fighting against God (theomachein) is a battle that cannot be won. This term 'adversus Deum pugnare' becomes a standard charge against persecutors.

key_terms.note: Theomachy — war against God. The most serious charge that can be leveled against a ruler.

verses.text_latin: Supra modum autem mater mirabilis et bonorum memoria digna quae pereuntes septem filios sub unius diei tempore conspiciens bono animo ferebat propter spem quam in Deum habebat.
verses.rendering: The mother was supremely admirable and worthy of blessed memory. Watching her seven sons perish within the space of a single day, she bore it with good courage because of the hope she had in God.
translator_notes: The narrator's tribute to the mother: 'supra modum mirabilis' (admirable beyond measure). She watches all seven sons die in one day and endures it through hope in God. This is the most extreme test of faith in the Bible.

key_terms.note: The highest superlative praise — the mother surpasses all human expectation.

key_terms.rendered_as: the hope she had in God
key_terms.note: Hope (spes) in God as the sustaining power through the worst suffering imaginable.

verses.text_latin: Singulos illorum hortabatur patria voce fortiter repleta sapientia et femineae cogitationi masculinum animum inserens.
verses.rendering: She encouraged each of them in the ancestral language, filled with courageous wisdom, and combining a woman's reasoning with a man's courage.
translator_notes: The mother speaks in Hebrew/Aramaic (patria voce), filled with wisdom and courage. The Latin text's 'femineae cogitationi masculinum animum inserens' reflects ancient gender categories — we render it noting the ancient framework while recognizing the mother's courage transcends such categories.

key_terms.note: Hebrew or Aramaic — the mother, like her sons, speaks the language of resistance.

verses.text_latin: Dixit autem eis: Nescio qualiter in utero meo apparuistis nec enim ego spiritum et animam donavi vobis et vitam et singulorum membra non ego ipsa compegi.
verses.rendering: She said to them, 'I do not know how you appeared in my womb; it was not I who gave you the breath of life and the soul, nor was it I who arranged the limbs of each of you.'
translator_notes: The mother's theological statement about human formation: she carried them but did not create them. 'Spiritum et animam' (spirit and soul) and 'singulorum membra' (each one's limbs) — the full person, spiritual and physical, is God's work, not the mother's. This is simultaneously a statement of humility about motherhood and a theological assertion about divine creativity.

key_terms.rendered_as: the breath of life and the soul
key_terms.note: The spiritual dimension of human existence — given by God, not by human parents.

key_terms.rendered_as: the limbs of each of you
key_terms.note: The physical body formed in the womb — divine craftsmanship, not mere biology.

verses.text_latin: Sed enim mundi Creator qui formavit hominis nativitatem quique omnium invenit originem et spiritum vobis iterum cum misericordia reddet et vitam sicut nunc vosmetipsos despicitis propter leges eius.
verses.rendering: Therefore the Creator of the world, who fashioned the birth of humankind and devised the origin of all things, will in his mercy give back to you again both breath and life, since you now despise yourselves for the sake of his laws.
translator_notes: THE creation-resurrection link: the God who created humanity will re-create the martyrs. 'Mundi Creator' (Creator of the world) connects resurrection to original creation — the same power that made life the first time will restore it. 'Cum misericordia' (with mercy) — resurrection is an act of divine compassion, not mere power.

key_terms.note: God as cosmic Creator — the title that grounds resurrection hope in creation power.
Resurrection as an act of divine mercy, not merely divine omnipotence.
The full restoration of the person — spirit and life returned by the same God who first gave them.

verses.text_latin: Antiochus autem contemni se arbitrans simul et exprobrantis voce despecta cum adhuc adulescentior superesset non solum verbis hortabatur sed et cum iuramento adfirmabat se divitem et beatum facturum et translatum a patriis legibus amicum habiturum et res necessarias ei praebiturum.
verses.rendering: Antiochus, thinking he was being treated with contempt, and suspecting that the voice of reproach was directed at him, while the youngest still survived, not only urged him with words but also assured him with an oath that he would make him rich and happy, and would count him as a friend if he turned from the ancestral laws, and would provide him with all he needed.
translator_notes: The king shifts strategy for the youngest: instead of torture, he offers wealth, happiness, friendship, and security. The temptation of the youngest is by seduction rather than force.

key_terms.rendered_as: if he turned from the ancestral laws
key_terms.note: The price of royal favor: apostasy from Torah.

verses.text_latin: Ad haec autem cum adulescens nequaquam inclinaretur vocavit matrem et suadebat ei ut adulescenti fieret in salutem.
verses.rendering: But when the young man would not be swayed at all, the king called the mother and urged her to counsel the youth for his salvation.
translator_notes: The king enlists the mother as his ally — hoping maternal love will break what royal power could not. This sets up the mother's greatest speech.

verses.text_latin: Cum autem multis eam verbis esset hortatus promisit suasuram se filio suo.
verses.rendering: After he had urged her at length, she promised that she would persuade her son.
translator_notes: The mother appears to agree — creating a moment of suspense. Will she betray her principles to save her last child?

verses.text_latin: Itaque inclinata ad illum inridens crudelem tyrannum ait patria voce: Fili mi miserere mei quae te in utero novem mensibus portavi et lac triennio dedi et alui et in aetatem istam perduxi.
verses.rendering: Leaning toward him, she mocked the cruel tyrant and said in the ancestral language, 'My son, have pity on me, who carried you in my womb for nine months, and nursed you for three years, and nourished you and brought you to this age.'
translator_notes: The mother's speech to her youngest — spoken in Hebrew/Aramaic so the king cannot understand — begins with an appeal to maternal bond. But the appeal is not to save his life; it is to secure his death. She asks him to pity her by dying faithfully, not by apostatizing.

key_terms.note: The mother speaks in Hebrew/Aramaic — a private channel the king cannot monitor. Her words of encouragement to die faithfully are hidden from the persecutor.

verses.text_latin: Peto nate ut aspicias ad caelum et terram et ad omnia quae in eis sunt et intellegas quia ex nihilo fecit illa Deus et hominum genus.
verses.rendering: 'I ask you, my child, to look at the heaven and the earth and all that is in them, and to understand that God made them from nothing, and the human race as well.'
translator_notes: THE verse: 'ex nihilo fecit illa Deus' — God made all things from nothing. This is the first explicit statement of creation ex nihilo in biblical literature. The mother's argument moves from observation (look at heaven and earth) to theology (God made them from nothing) to application (therefore God can remake your body from nothing). This single verse became the foundation of the Christian doctrine of creation ex nihilo, articulated in the Nicene Creed and defended by Irenaeus, Augustine, and Aquinas.

key_terms.note: Creation ex nihilo — the foundational metaphysical claim that God created all things not from pre-existing matter but from absolute nothing. The single most influential phrase in the deuterocanonical literature.
Humanity included in the scope of creation from nothing — human existence is entirely dependent on divine will.

verses.text_latin: Ita fiet ut non timeas carnificem istum sed dignus fratribus tuis effectus particeps suscipe mortem ut in illa miseratione cum fratribus tuis te recipiam.
verses.rendering: 'So do not fear this executioner, but be worthy of your brothers. Accept death, so that in God's mercy I may receive you back again with your brothers.'
translator_notes: The mother's final request: do not fear death; be worthy of your brothers; accept death. 'In illa miseratione te recipiam' (in that mercy I may receive you back) — she expects to be reunited with all seven sons in the resurrection. This is maternal hope projected into eternity.

key_terms.note: The mercy of the resurrection — the mother expects to receive her sons back through God's compassionate restoration of life.

verses.text_latin: Cum haec illa adhuc diceret ait adulescens: Quem sustinetis? Non oboedio praecepto regis sed praecepto legis quae data est nobis per Moysen.
verses.rendering: While she was still speaking, the young man said, 'What are you waiting for? I do not obey the command of the king, but the command of the law that was given to us through Moses.'
translator_notes: The youngest brother speaks with the most confident defiance of all: 'What are you waiting for?' He directly contrasts royal command with divine command — and chooses divine command.

key_terms.note: The Torah's command as the supreme authority, overriding royal edicts.

verses.text_latin: Tu vero qui inventor omnis malitiae factus es in Hebraeos non effugies manum Dei.
verses.rendering: 'But you, who have become the author of all wickedness against the Hebrews, you will not escape the hand of God.'
translator_notes: The youngest directly accuses the king: 'inventor omnis malitiae' (author of all wickedness). The threat is the same as Eleazar's and the other brothers': God's hand is inescapable.

key_terms.note: The divine hand of judgment — the power that no human authority can evade.

verses.text_latin: Nos enim pro peccatis nostris haec patimur.
verses.rendering: 'For we suffer these things because of our own sins.'
translator_notes: Like the sixth brother, the youngest acknowledges the penitential dimension: their suffering has a covenantal cause in Israel's sins.

verses.text_latin: Et si nobis propter increpationem et correptionem Dominus Deus noster modicum iratus est sed iterum reconciliabitur servis suis.
verses.rendering: 'And if the Lord our God has been briefly angry with us, for the sake of rebuke and correction, he will again be reconciled with his servants.'
translator_notes: The theology is nuanced: God's anger is 'modicum' (brief, limited), directed at correction not destruction, and will end in reconciliation. This echoes 6:12-16.

key_terms.note: Two forms of divine discipline: verbal rebuke and corrective action — both temporary.
The restoration of right relationship between God and Israel — the ultimate hope.

verses.text_latin: Tu autem o sceleste et omnium hominum flagitiosissime noli frustra extolli vanis spebus in servos eius inflammatus.
verses.rendering: 'But you, wicked and most vile of all mortals, do not be vainly puffed up with empty hopes, inflamed against his servants.'
translator_notes: The youngest brother's denunciation of Antiochus reaches its climax: 'sceleste et flagitiosissime' (wicked and most vile). His 'hopes' are empty; his fury against God's servants is futile.

verses.text_latin: Nondum enim omnipotentis Dei et omnia conspicientis iudicium effugisti.
verses.rendering: 'For you have not yet escaped the judgment of almighty God, who sees all things.'
translator_notes: God as 'omnipotens' (almighty) and 'omnia conspiciens' (all-seeing) — the two attributes that make divine judgment inescapable. Power to execute judgment and knowledge of all deeds.

key_terms.rendered_as: almighty God, who sees all things
key_terms.note: Omnipotence and omniscience together — the foundation of certain divine judgment.

verses.text_latin: Nam fratres mei modico nunc dolore sustentato sub testamento aeternae vitae effecti sunt. Tu vero iudicio Dei iustas superbiae tuae poenas exsolves.
verses.rendering: 'For my brothers, having endured a brief suffering, have now fallen under God's covenant of everlasting life. But you, by the judgment of God, will pay the just penalties for your arrogance.'
translator_notes: The contrast is absolute: the brothers' suffering is 'brief' (modico) and leads to 'eternal life' (aeternae vitae); the king's arrogance leads to just punishment. 'Sub testamento aeternae vitae' (under the covenant of everlasting life) — the brothers' death brings them into an eternal covenant.

key_terms.note: The eternal covenant — the brothers' martyrdom places them under a covenant that transcends death.

verses.text_latin: Ego autem sicut et fratres mei animam et corpus meum trado pro patriis legibus invocans Deum maturius genti nostrae propitium fieri teque cum tormentis et verberibus confiteri quod ipse est Deus solus.
verses.rendering: 'But I, like my brothers, surrender my soul and my body for the ancestral laws, calling upon God to show mercy to our nation speedily, and that you, through torments and afflictions, may confess that he alone is God.'
translator_notes: The youngest brother's final words: (1) he surrenders body and soul; (2) he prays for the nation's deliverance; (3) he prophesies that the king himself will eventually confess God's sovereignty — through his own suffering. This prophecy is fulfilled in chapter 9.

key_terms.note: The total self-offering — both spiritual and physical existence surrendered for the Torah.
The monotheistic confession — the Shema rendered as the martyr's dying declaration.

verses.text_latin: In me vero et in fratribus meis desinet Omnipotentis ira quae super omne genus nostrum iuste superducta est.
verses.rendering: 'But in me and in my brothers, the wrath of the Almighty, which has been justly brought upon our whole nation, will come to an end.'
translator_notes: The youngest brother's most extraordinary claim: his death and his brothers' deaths will exhaust God's wrath against the nation. Their suffering is vicarious — they absorb the divine anger so that it does not fall on others. This theology of vicarious atoning suffering became profoundly influential in Christian atonement theology.

key_terms.rendered_as: the wrath of the Almighty will come to an end
key_terms.note: The martyrs' deaths as the terminus of divine wrath — vicarious, atoning suffering that absorbs punishment on behalf of the nation.

verses.text_latin: Tunc rex accensus ira in hunc super omnes crudelius desaevit indigne ferens se derisum.
verses.rendering: Then the king, burning with rage, vented his fury on this one more cruelly than all the others, unable to bear being mocked.
translator_notes: The king's response to the youngest brother's defiance is the most extreme cruelty — and it is driven by wounded pride, not policy. 'Indigne ferens se derisum' (unable to bear being mocked) — the tyrant is controlled by his ego.

verses.text_latin: Et hic itaque mundus obiit per omnia in Domino confidens.
verses.rendering: And so this one too died pure, trusting wholly in the Lord.
translator_notes: 'Mundus' (clean, pure) — the youngest dies ritually and morally pure, having refused the defiling pork. 'Per omnia in Domino confidens' (trusting wholly in the Lord) — total faith in God as the final state of the martyr.

key_terms.note: Ritual and moral purity maintained through death — the whole point of the martyrdom.
Trust in God as the final disposition of the dying martyr.

verses.text_latin: Novissime autem post filios et mater consumpta est.
verses.rendering: Last of all, after her sons, the mother also died.
translator_notes: The mother's death is recorded in a single sentence — the most understated line in the chapter. After all the speeches and theologies, the narrator simply says: 'and the mother also died.' The brevity honors the enormity of what she endured.

verses.text_latin: Igitur de sacrificiis et de nimiis crudelitatibus satis dictum est.
verses.rendering: So let this be enough about the sacrificial meals and the extreme cruelties.
translator_notes: The narrator closes the martyrdom section with deliberate restraint: 'enough has been said.' The horrors speak for themselves. The transition leads to the Maccabean military resistance.
